title: Testing a document on someone who was not there
lead: Use it when you wrote something for people who were not in the room, because you can no longer judge your own draft: you know what every shortcut means.
produces: A document that fresh readers with no context could follow, plus a record of each finding you accepted or rejected and why.
scenario: You drafted a one-page proposal asking the lab heads' committee to approve a four-week pilot of Run comparison v1. One committee member is a lab head from a different discipline who has never seen a reference run.
input: Here is my one-pager for the lab heads' committee. Read it cold and tell me what a stranger would not follow.

steps.label: Say who reads it and what they decide
steps.text: You write one line first: a lab head from another discipline reads this for three minutes and decides whether to approve a four-week pilot. Readers are held to that line. Without it they can only comment on style.

steps.label: First fresh reader
steps.text: A reader with no access to your notes or earlier drafts reads the page once. Four findings come back: "reference run" is never defined, "tolerance" appears as a percentage and as a count, the pilot's cost to the assay team is in the last line, and nobody is named who can stop the pilot. You wrote the page and found none of these.

steps.label: Accept or reject each finding
steps.text: You accept three and reject one. The reader wanted the full instrument list; the committee decides on scope, so you say the pilot covers two instruments. You define both terms in one sentence each, move the cost to the top and name who can stop the pilot. A rejection needs a reason.

steps.label: A new reader, a new context
steps.text: A new reader sees only the revised page. A reader who saw the first version would be checking your fixes instead of reading. This round finds one new problem: the pilot dates do not say which weeks. You fix it and call another round.

steps.label: A finding reverses an earlier rejection
steps.text: The next reader asks for the instrument list you rejected in round one. Findings that keep changing mean the page is not settled, so you keep going, up to the round limit you set at the start. The limit is a design choice. Without one the loop has no end.

steps.label: Repeat until findings stop changing
steps.text: You add one line about the instruments. The final reader finds nothing new and repeats no earlier finding. The loop works on a local file throughout, and nothing is published or sent until this gate passes.

steps.label: The converged page and the record
steps.text: You have the final one-pager and a list of findings by round, each marked accepted, rejected with a reason, or still open. A person sends it. The method never does.

settled: "Reference run" and "tolerance" are defined where they first appear.
The pilot's cost to the assay team is in the first paragraph.
The pilot covers two of the three instruments, and the page says so.
open: Whether the committee wants the full instrument list. One reader asked twice; the other readers did not.

artifact.title: Round record excerpt
lines: Round 1, finding 1. "Reference run" never defined. Accepted: defined in the second sentence.
Round 1, finding 3. Add the full instrument list. Rejected: the committee decides on scope, not on hardware.
Round 2, finding 1. Pilot weeks not stated. Accepted: dates added.
Round 3, finding 1. Instrument list requested again. Accepted in part: one line naming the two instruments.
Round 4. No new findings; none repeated. Ready for you to send.

stop: Stop when a fresh reader finds nothing new and repeats no earlier finding, or when you reach the round limit. If the limit arrives first, the open findings come back to you, and you decide whether the page is good enough to send.
limits: The readers are agents. They catch missing context and unclear terms. They cannot tell you whether the committee will approve, and they do not grade the argument. A lab head reading the page once is still the better test of whether it works.
